questions.q: According to popular legend, Liechtenstein’s last army went to war in 1866 with 80 men and came home with?
questions.e: Nobody fired a shot, and the extra man was supposedly a new friend. It’s a legend, but nobody wants to disprove it.

questions.q: Japanese officer Hiroo Onoda kept fighting World War II in the Philippine jungle until?
questions.e: He refused to believe the war had ended until his former commander flew in to relieve him of duty.

questions.q: How did the career of Zheng Yi Sao, the powerful 19th-century Chinese pirate commander, end?
questions.a: She negotiated a deal and retired rich
w: She was captured by the British
questions.e: She commanded hundreds of ships, beat fleets sent to stop her, and got away with her loot. She then ran a gambling house.

questions.q: In 1859, San Francisco businessman Joshua Norton declared himself?
questions.e: The city played along, honouring his homemade money. Thousands of people came to his funeral.

questions.q: Was Napoleon really unusually short?
w: Yes, but only in old age
questions.e: He was around 170 cm, average for his day. Confused units and British cartoons did the rest.

questions.q: In 1712, because of a calendar muddle, Sweden had which date?
questions.e: Sweden switched calendars badly, then switched back. It needed a leap day on top of a leap day.

questions.q: In the Netherlands’ ‘tulip mania’ of 1637, the prices of tulip bulbs?
questions.e: Some rare bulbs sold for more than a craftsman’s yearly wage. Historians think tales of total ruin were overblown.

questions.q: Nobel Prizes are presented on 10 December because that’s the date when Alfred Nobel?
questions.e: He died in 1896. Stockholm has since marked the date with medals and a very long dinner.

questions.q: In 1940, as Nazi troops took Copenhagen, chemist George de Hevesy hid two Nobel gold medals by?
questions.e: The liquid sat on a lab shelf all war. Afterwards, the gold was recovered and the medals were recast.

questions.q: In 2004, who became the first African woman to win a Nobel Peace Prize, partly for planting trees?
questions.e: Her Green Belt Movement in Kenya has planted tens of millions of trees.

questions.q: Winston Churchill won a Nobel Prize in 1953. In which category?
questions.e: For his histories and speeches. He was busy, so his wife Clementine collected it in Stockholm.

questions.q: Who is the only person to have won two unshared Nobel Prizes?
questions.e: Chemistry in 1954 and Peace in 1962. Curie shared her first one, so she just misses out.

questions.q: How many Nobel Peace Prizes did Mahatma Gandhi win?
questions.e: He was nominated five times. The committee has publicly regretted this omission.

questions.q: Barbara McClintock’s 1983 Nobel Prize for ‘jumping genes’ came from decades of studying?
questions.e: Many scientists doubted her in the 1950s. She kept going with her corn and was proved right.

questions.q: Nominations for Nobel Prizes are kept secret for how long?
questions.e: So you won’t find out for decades that your uncle didn’t really get nominated.

questions.q: The menu at the Nobel Banquet in Stockholm is kept secret until?
questions.e: About 1300 guests sit down without knowing what’s coming. Fancy way to do a mystery meal.

questions.q: At the 2010 Peace Prize ceremony, the winner was represented by?
questions.e: Chinese writer Liu Xiaobo was in prison, and no family member was allowed to go. The empty chair became a famous image.

questions.q: Why does a sealed chips packet puff up on a mountain?
w: The cold makes the bag expand
questions.e: The air inside stays put while the air outside thins out. Your snack hasn’t changed; the atmosphere has.

questions.q: Measured from its base to its top, the world’s tallest mountain is?
questions.e: Most of this Hawaiian volcano sits underwater, and it’s over 10,000 m from base to peak. Everest wins only above sea level.

questions.q: The point on Earth’s surface furthest from the planet’s centre is the top of?
questions.e: Earth bulges at the equator, giving this Ecuadorian peak a boost. Geography is full of technicalities.

questions.q: In 1975, who became the first woman to climb Everest?
questions.e: She’d survived an avalanche on the way up, and later became the first woman to climb the highest peak on every continent.

questions.q: The Indian mathematician who calculated in 1852 that Everest was the world’s highest peak was?
questions.e: George Everest, who gave his name to the peak, never climbed it. He also said his surname ‘Eve-rest’.

questions.q: On the summit in 1953, Tenzing Norgay buried what as an offering?
questions.e: Edmund Hillary left a small cross. On top of the world, a chocolate is a real sacrifice.

questions.q: Which bird migrates right across the Himalayas, flying thousands of metres up?
questions.e: Its blood is unusually good at holding on to oxygen. It sometimes makes the climb by night.

questions.q: At the summit of Everest, water boils at about?
questions.e: Low pressure means low boiling points, so that’s a pretty sad cup of tea.

questions.q: Many Tibetans’ ability to cope at altitude comes partly from a gene variant passed on by?
questions.e: Their ancient relatives, the Denisovans, interbred with modern humans. Genetics got very weird in 2014.

questions.q: Mount Everest is still?
questions.a: Growing by a few millimetres a year
w: Shrinking by a metre a year
questions.e: India is still crashing into Asia, pushing the Himalayas upward. Climbers, your record may need updating.

theme: Health for all, around the world

questions.q: The UK’s National Health Service opened in 1948. The first person it treated was?
questions.e: Sylvia Diggory was treated in Manchester. She was reportedly told she was making history, which is a lot at 13.

questions.q: Which country created the first national sickness insurance scheme, in 1883?
questions.e: Otto von Bismarck was the man behind it. Other countries gradually followed the idea.

questions.q: Workers who built the pharaohs’ tombs at Deir el-Medina in Egypt seem to have had?
questions.a: Paid sick days and a doctor
questions.e: Ancient records and skeletons suggest a form of health care about 3200 years ago. Some sick days were for brewing beer, apparently.

questions.q: Which country abolished its army in the late 1940s and put more money into health and education?
questions.e: It’s still without a standing army. Its people live longer than you’d expect from its wealth.

questions.q: Bhutan, whose constitution promises free basic health care, is also famous for measuring?
questions.e: The small Himalayan country decided wealth wasn’t all that mattered.

questions.q: John Flynn started which famous health service in outback Australia in 1928?
questions.e: The first flight left from Cloncurry in Queensland. It covers an area bigger than most countries.

questions.q: Jamaican-Scottish businesswoman Mary Seacole paid her own way to the Crimean War, where she opened?
questions.e: Officially she’d been turned down. So she went anyway, and fed and cared for the soldiers near the front.

questions.q: China’s ‘barefoot doctors’ of the 1960s and 70s were?
questions.a: Farmers trained in basic health care
questions.e: Many worked in the rice fields as well as caring for villagers, hence the nickname.

questions.q: The famous 1978 ‘Health for All’ declaration was made in Alma-Ata, in what is now?
questions.e: Today the city is called Almaty. Astana’s the capital, in case you forgot October’s quiz.

questions.q: Since 2016, Rwanda has been famous for delivering urgent blood supplies by?
questions.e: Zipline parachutes packages down from the sky. It was the world’s first national drone delivery service.

questions.q: In 1947, Claude Beck restarted a human heart with an electric shock for the first time. Whose heart was it?
questions.e: The boy recovered and went home. It happened in Cleveland, Ohio.

questions.q: The Resusci Anne CPR doll has a face based on?
questions.a: The reputed death mask of an unknown woman in Paris
w: A portrait of its maker’s Norwegian wife
An old Greek statue of a goddess
A fairy tale character from Germany
questions.e: Toy maker Asmund Laerdal recognised the serene mask. It’s been called the most-kissed face of all time.

questions.q: CPR trainers often say to press in time to which Bee Gees song?
questions.e: At about 103 beats a minute it’s just right, and also impossible to forget.

questions.q: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani famously used electricity to make what twitch?
questions.e: His wife Lucia helped with the work, and his name gave us ‘galvanise’.

questions.q: In 1803 at Newgate in London, Giovanni Aldini shocked audiences by?
questions.a: Running electricity through a hanged man’s body
w: Lighting up a street with electric eels
Bringing a mouse back to life with a spark
Curing a blind man with a battery
questions.e: The jaw and an eye moved. The show may well have helped inspire Frankenstein.

questions.q: In about 46 CE, Roman writer Scribonius Largus suggested people with headaches should?
w: Hold an iron bar in the sea
questions.e: It’s one of the first known uses of electricity to make someone feel better. Results not guaranteed.

questions.q: Electric eels, which can deliver over 800 volts, are actually?
questions.e: They’re freshwater fish from South America. The name is misleading, and so is the idea you should touch one.

questions.q: Prototypes of the first implanted pacemaker in Sweden in 1958 were moulded using?
questions.e: Else-Marie Larsson talked the team into trying it on her husband, Arne. He went on to outlive both of the men who built it.

questions.q: Wilson Greatbatch stumbled on the idea for his 1950s pacemaker when he?
questions.a: Used the wrong resistor in a circuit
w: Spilled coffee on a radio set
Got a static shock from a door
Heard a clock ticking through a wall
questions.e: The circuit started pulsing like a heartbeat. He knew straight away what it could do.

questions.q: The first portable defibrillator, built in Belfast in 1965, ran on?
questions.e: Frank Pantridge’s machine weighed about 70 kg. Heart emergencies had a new home: the back of an ambulance.

questions.q: Which creature was once widely used to drain people’s blood?
questions.e: At the height of the craze, France imported millions of leeches a year.

questions.q: Which US president died on this day in 1799, after heavy bloodletting for a very sore throat?
questions.e: Up to 40% of his blood may have been taken in a day. It’s hard to imagine it helped.

questions.q: The original Chinese ‘snake oil’, brought to the USA by railway workers, was made from which snake?
questions.e: The real stuff was rich in omega-3 oils. American copies used rattlesnakes, or no snake at all, which is how ‘snake oil’ came to mean a con.

questions.q: Expensive ‘unicorn horn’, thought to cure poisons, was really the tusk of a?
questions.e: Queen Elizabeth I reportedly owned one worth a fortune. It was a whale’s tooth.

questions.q: In medieval and early modern Europe, people could buy medicine made from?
questions.e: Ground-up mummy was a real trade for centuries. The mummies were real; the benefits were not.

questions.q: The red and white stripes on a barber’s pole come from when barbers?
questions.e: Haircuts, tooth-pulling and surgery were once all in a day’s work. Would you like a trim with that?

questions.q: In 18th-century London, what was blown up a drowned person’s bottom to try to revive them?
questions.e: Kits with bellows were kept beside the River Thames. People really did believe in it for decades.

questions.q: How have archaeologists traced the campsites of American explorers Lewis and Clark?
questions.e: They took laxative pills laced with mercury, nicknamed ‘thunderclappers’. Their journey left a toxic trail.

questions.q: ‘Trepanning’, one of humanity’s oldest procedures, means?
questions.a: Drilling a hole in the skull
questions.e: Healed skulls show people often survived it, thousands of years ago.

questions.q: Victorian ‘complexion wafers’ sold to women promised lovely skin, but contained?
questions.e: Pale skin was the fashion, and arsenic really could give a pallor, at a terrible cost.

questions.q: Esperanto’s creator, L. L. Zamenhof, born today in 1859, worked as?
questions.e: He hoped a shared language would ease the conflict he saw between communities in his home town of Białystok.

questions.q: ‘Esperanto’ means?
questions.e: His pen name was ‘Doktoro Esperanto’. The word then became the name of the whole language.

questions.q: On La Gomera in the Canary Islands, people can talk across deep valleys using?
questions.e: Silbo Gomero is taught in the island’s schools and can carry for kilometres.

questions.q: Which country has more languages than any other, with over 800?
questions.e: Mountains and islands kept communities apart, so languages multiplied. Good luck with the phrasebook.

questions.q: A person who loves words is a?
questions.e: From Greek logos, ‘word’, and philos, ‘loving’. A bibliophile loves books, an audiophile loves good sound, and a logophobe would hate this quiz.

questions.q: ‘Ketchup’ likely comes from a word in the Hokkien language of southern China for?
questions.e: It reached Britain with traders long before anyone thought of adding tomatoes.

questions.q: The word ‘emoji’ has nothing to do with ‘emotion’. It comes from Japanese for?
questions.e: E + moji. The resemblance to ‘emotion’ is a total coincidence.

questions.q: Myth says ‘kangaroo’ means ‘I don’t know’. It really comes from a Guugu Yimithirr word for?
questions.e: Captain Cook’s crew wrote it down in 1770. The ‘I don’t know’ story is a myth that refuses to hop away.

questions.q: The word ‘OK’ began in 1839 as a joke abbreviation of?
questions.e: Boston newspapers were having a craze for silly misspelled initials. Only this one survived.

questions.q: Nüshu, from Hunan in China, is a writing system created and used only by?
questions.e: For centuries, women shared poems and letters in it, while men largely ignored it.

theme: Beethoven and the brain on music

questions.q: Beethoven was almost certainly born in December 1770, but we don’t know the exact day because the record shows only his?
questions.e: He was baptised on 17 December in Bonn, so a birthday of 16 December is a good guess.

questions.q: Which city was Beethoven born in?
questions.e: He moved to Vienna at about 21 and never moved back. West Germany’s later capital was his home town.

questions.q: To hear his piano as his deafness grew, Beethoven is said to have?
questions.a: Bitten a rod attached to it
w: Put his ear to the floor
questions.e: The vibrations travel through the jaw to the inner ear. It’s called bone conduction.

questions.q: At the 1824 premiere of the Ninth Symphony, contralto Caroline Unger is said to have?
questions.a: Turned Beethoven to see the applause
w: Sung the whole work in Italian
Stopped the concert to thank him
questions.e: He was still facing the orchestra and couldn’t hear the crowd.

questions.q: ‘Für Elise’ is one of the world’s best-known piano pieces. Who was Elise?
questions.e: The name may even have been a misreading of ‘Therese’.

questions.q: Beethoven dedicated his ‘Eroica’ symphony to which leader, then scratched out the name?
questions.e: He was furious when Napoleon crowned himself emperor. The title page still has the hole he made.

questions.q: Beethoven’s coffee was reportedly made with exactly how many beans a cup?
questions.e: He’s said to have counted them himself. Early hipster.

questions.q: The famous ‘Hiller lock’ of Beethoven’s hair, cut from his head as the story went, was DNA tested in 2023. It turned out to?
questions.e: Lots of the claims made about his health based on that lock had to be rethought.

questions.q: Scottish percussionist Evelyn Glennie, profoundly deaf since about age 12, usually performs?
questions.e: She says she hears through her whole body, feeling the vibrations in the floor.

questions.q: In World War II, the opening of Beethoven’s Fifth became a symbol for the Allies because?
questions.a: Its rhythm is the Morse code for V
w: It sounds like a marching band
questions.e: Short-short-short-long is V, for victory. The BBC used it in its broadcasts to occupied Europe.

questions.q: The Wright brothers’ first powered flight on this day in 1903 lasted?
questions.e: It covered about 37 metres, which is shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.

questions.q: What was the Wright brothers’ business before aviation?
questions.e: Light frames, chains and balance all came in handy.

questions.q: Why was it Orville at the controls on 17 December?
questions.a: Wilbur had his go on 14 December and stalled
w: Orville had paid for the plane
questions.e: A coin toss gave Wilbur the first try, and it was too short to count. So it was Orville’s turn.

questions.q: A piece of the Wright Flyer’s fabric was later carried on?
questions.e: Just 66 years separated those two events. The fabric and some wood went along with Neil Armstrong.

questions.q: Katharine Wright, the brothers’ sister, helped by?
questions.a: Managing their affairs and charming Europe
questions.e: A teacher, she ran things at home, then joined them in France, where she became a celebrity herself.

questions.q: In 1921, Bessie Coleman became the first Black and Native American woman to earn a pilot’s licence. Where did she train?
questions.e: US flying schools wouldn’t take her, so she learned French and moved to France.

questions.q: Your ears pop on a plane because?
questions.a: Air pressure inside your ears changes
w: The cabin air is too dry
questions.e: Swallowing or yawning opens a small tube in your ear, which lets the pressure even out.

questions.q: Jet lag is generally worse when you fly?
questions.e: Your body clock finds it easier to stretch a day than shorten one.

questions.q: The first passengers on a Montgolfier hot air balloon, in 1783, were?
questions.a: A sheep, a duck and a rooster
w: The king and queen of France
questions.e: They landed safely. It was a test to see if air travel could be survived by living things, with animals as the volunteers.

questions.q: Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont helped popularise what, so he could check the time while flying?
questions.e: His friend Louis Cartier made him one because a pocket watch was too hard to reach mid-air.

theme: Food and ideas on the move

questions.q: Japanese tempura owes its origins to?
questions.e: They arrived in the 1500s with batter-fried fish. Japan kept it and perfected it.

questions.q: Fried fish, half of Britain’s national dish, was brought there by?
questions.a: Jewish refugees from Spain and Portugal
w: French monks after the Battle of Hastings
Sailors from the Dutch East Indies
questions.e: Sephardic Jews had long fried fish before the Sabbath. Then someone added chips.

questions.q: Fortune cookies, a staple of Chinese restaurants in the USA, seem to have come from?
questions.e: Similar crackers were made near a Kyoto shrine, and Japanese American bakers brought them to California.

questions.q: Before the 1500s, what did Indian and Thai food never contain, because it hadn’t arrived from the Americas?
questions.e: Spice-loving Asia learned chilli from Portuguese ships. Black pepper had to do the job before then.

questions.q: Levi Strauss, who co-patented riveted jeans in 1873, was born in what is now which country?
questions.e: Strauss came from Bavaria and Davis from Riga. American as apple pie, which isn’t that American either.

questions.q: The number symbols we call ‘Arabic’ actually began in?
questions.e: Mathematicians in Baghdad picked them up from India and passed them on to Europe.

questions.q: Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara on which island, before his family moved to England?
questions.e: His Parsi family fled the 1964 revolution. A rock star got a very long route to London.

questions.q: Physicist Lise Meitner fled the Nazis in 1938. A few months later, on a snowy walk in Sweden, she worked out?
questions.e: Her former colleague Otto Hahn won the Nobel Prize. She didn’t, despite many nominations.

questions.q: Before the 2016 Olympics, Syrian refugee Yusra Mardini saved people by?
questions.a: Pushing a sinking boat to shore
questions.e: She and her sister swam for hours pulling a dinghy to Greece. Then she swam for the Refugee Olympic Team in Rio.

questions.q: Why do some languages say ‘tea’ and others say ‘chai’?
questions.a: They got it by sea or by land
w: Hot and cold brews have separate names
It depends how much milk is added
questions.e: Sea traders spread a word from coastal Fujian, while overland traders spread the word from the rest of China.

questions.q: A Christmas Carol was published on this day in 1843. Dickens wrote it in about?
questions.e: He was also writing Martin Chuzzlewit at the same time, and needed the money.

questions.q: Dickens’s pet raven, Grip, helped inspire which poem by Edgar Allan Poe?
questions.e: Poe reviewed Barnaby Rudge, which featured Grip. When the bird died, Dickens had him stuffed. You can still see him in Philadelphia.

questions.q: What did ‘humbug’ mean when Scrooge said it?
questions.e: It’s a fraud or nonsense, rather than a mint-flavoured lolly. Scrooge wasn’t cross at confectionery.

questions.q: Before settling on Tiny Tim, Dickens wrote his character’s name in the manuscript as?
questions.e: He crossed it out and later gave ‘Fred’ to Scrooge’s jolly nephew.

questions.q: Despite huge sales, Dickens made less than expected from the first edition because?
questions.a: He insisted on a lavish book at a low price
w: A pirate press stole all the copies
He gave every copy to charity
questions.e: Hand-coloured plates and gilt edges ate his profit, and he got about £230 instead of the £1000 he hoped for.

questions.q: How many ghosts visit Scrooge altogether?
questions.e: Everyone forgets Marley. Past, Present and Yet to Come make up the rest.

questions.q: Bob Cratchit’s wage in the story is?
questions.e: ‘Bob’ was slang for a shilling, and Bob was only paid 15 of them. Dickens loved a pun.

questions.q: Who played Ebenezer Scrooge in The Muppet Christmas Carol?
questions.e: He played it totally straight, as if working with the Royal Shakespeare Company. It’s why it works.

questions.q: A Christmas Carol’s first line ends: ‘Marley was dead’?
questions.e: ‘Dead as a door-nail’ comes a few lines later. Tricky, yes.

questions.q: Dickens helped wealthy heiress Angela Burdett-Coutts run Urania Cottage, a home for?
questions.e: She was one of the richest women in Britain and gave most of it away. He handled the day-to-day.

questions.q: Antarctica’s ‘Blood Falls’ are red because the water contains?
questions.e: The salty, iron-rich water turns rust-red when it hits the air. Its discoverers first blamed algae.

questions.q: In which country has the ‘Door to Hell’, a burning gas crater, been on fire for decades?
questions.e: It’s usually said that Soviet engineers set it alight to burn off the gas, assuming it would go out in a few weeks.

questions.q: ‘Anatidaephobia’, the fear that somewhere, somehow, a duck is watching you, was invented by?
questions.a: Gary Larson, in The Far Side
questions.e: It’s a joke phobia from a Far Side cartoon, not a real diagnosis. Larson also gave us luposlipaphobia: fear of being chased by wolves round a table while wearing socks on a polished floor.

questions.q: Fossil hunter Mary Anning helped work out that strange ‘bezoar stones’ found in Dorset were?
questions.e: Coprolites, to be polite. She’d found an ichthyosaur skeleton when she was about 12.

questions.q: Pando in Utah, which looks like a whole aspen forest, is actually?
questions.e: About 47,000 trunks with one root system, all genetically identical. It’s one of the heaviest living things on Earth.

questions.q: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast that the bubble it creates briefly gets as hot as?
questions.e: The bubble collapses in an instant, and it’s loud too. It’s a stunning way to catch dinner.

questions.q: Félicette, who went to space in 1963, was the first?
questions.e: France launched this Paris street cat on a short flight, and she came back alive. She finally got a statue in 2019.

questions.q: The Greenland shark is thought to live for up to about?
questions.e: Some alive today were swimming when Newton was a boy. They only become adults at about 150.

questions.q: Mike, a chicken in 1940s Colorado, became famous for?
questions.a: Living for 18 months without a head
w: Laying a record 90 eggs in a week
Crowing in tune with the radio
Being elected mayor of his town
questions.e: The axe missed the brain stem. He toured the USA, and his town now holds a festival.

questions.q: Hero of Alexandria designed which surprisingly modern gadget about 2000 years ago?
questions.e: Drop in a coin and it dispensed holy water. Yes, the first vending machine was for holy water.

questions.q: The UN’s World Meditation Day falls today, right around the December?
questions.e: It’s the longest night in one half of the world and the longest day in the other. Take your pick.

questions.q: About how many breaths does an adult take in a day?
questions.e: No, you don’t need to count them. That would be meditation, though.

questions.q: At any given moment, you’re probably breathing mostly through?
questions.e: It’s called the nasal cycle. Your nostrils take turns every few hours, without asking you.

questions.q: In a 2013 study, Tibetan nuns meditating in icy weather were able to?
questions.a: Dry wet sheets with body heat
w: Hold their breath for an hour
Stop their hearts for a minute
questions.e: Their temperature rose as high as 38.3°C. The rest of us just shiver.

questions.q: Studies suggest your yawn can be ‘caught’ by which pet?
questions.e: Dogs may catch more yawns from owners than from strangers. Sorry if you just yawned.

questions.q: Sperm whales nap in short bursts while?
questions.e: Picture a group of giant whales asleep like skittles standing on end. That’s real.

questions.q: Which animal sleeps or dozes for up to 20 hours or more a day?
questions.e: Gum leaves take lots of energy to digest. Koalas could teach a class on sitting still.

questions.q: Your heart gently slows as you?
questions.e: It speeds up slightly on the in-breath and slows on the out-breath. This is why long, slow breaths feel so calming.

questions.q: In 1968, the Beatles famously went to Rishikesh to study meditation, in which country?
questions.e: They wrote a lot of The White Album there. Ringo reportedly brought his own baked beans.

questions.q: Do you need to empty your mind to meditate?
w: Yes, for at least an hour
questions.e: Most methods are about noticing your thoughts, not stopping them. Good news for overthinkers.

questions.q: Self-taught maths genius Srinivasa Ramanujan, born today in 1887, came from which country?
questions.e: Today is National Mathematics Day in India, in his honour.

questions.q: What was the number of the taxi Ramanujan was told was ‘rather dull’, which he said was fascinating?
questions.e: It’s the smallest number you can make by adding two cubes in two different ways. As one does, while recovering in bed.

questions.q: Ramanujan said many of his formulas came to him in?
questions.e: He described seeing them unfold in sleep. Very few mathematicians’ dreams are as useful.

questions.q: Ramanujan wrote a letter full of amazing formulas to G. H. Hardy, a professor at which university?
questions.e: Hardy first suspected a hoax, then decided nobody could make up maths that good.

questions.q: Ramanujan often did his sums on a slate rather than paper because?
w: He loved the sound of chalk
questions.e: He would rub out his working with his elbow, so few of his steps survive.

questions.q: Which actor played Ramanujan in the 2015 film The Man Who Knew Infinity?
questions.e: Jeremy Irons played Hardy. Maths movies don’t often make you tear up, but here we are.

questions.q: Shakuntala Devi, India’s ‘human computer’, stunned London in 1980 by multiplying two 13-digit numbers in?
questions.e: She got it right and entered the record books, and her answer was on the board faster than most people can write it.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win the Fields Medal, the top prize in maths, in 2014?
questions.e: She grew up in Iran and worked by doodling on huge sheets of paper spread across her floor.

questions.q: Count the spirals on a sunflower’s head and you’ll usually find numbers from?
questions.e: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on. Each is the sum of the two before. Nature does maths too.

questions.q: Snakes and Ladders began in India as?
questions.e: Ladders were virtues and snakes were vices. Britain picked it up in Victorian times.

questions.q: Joseph Murray, the surgeon behind the first successful kidney transplant in 1954, later won?
questions.e: With an identical twin, the body doesn’t reject the organ. Dr Joseph Murray later got a Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Identical twins share almost all their DNA, but do they have the same fingerprints?
questions.e: Fingerprints are shaped by tiny pressures in the womb. So forensic teams can tell them apart.

questions.q: Igbo-Ora in Nigeria proudly calls itself the?
questions.e: It even holds a twins festival. Locals credit their diet, but no one is sure why.

questions.q: The nine-banded armadillo usually gives birth to?
questions.e: One egg splits into four, every time. Scientists love them for that.

questions.q: NASA studied identical twins Scott and Mark Kelly to see how a year in space affected?
questions.e: Mark stayed on Earth while Scott spent almost a year in orbit. Most changes returned to normal after he came back.

questions.q: Which twins, according to legend, founded Rome after being raised by a she-wolf?
questions.e: It didn’t end well for Remus. Sibling rivalry does get out of hand.

questions.q: The private language that some young twins invent together is called?
questions.e: Usually it’s just baby talk they understand between them, and most twins grow out of it.

questions.q: Which sisters shared the role of Michelle in the TV show Full House?
questions.e: Child labour laws limit a baby’s work hours, so twins are a TV producer’s favourite trick.

questions.q: Christiaan Barnard led the world’s first human heart transplant in 1967 in?
questions.e: Louis Washkansky lived 18 days. The next recipient lived for over a year and a half. The city still has a museum about it.

questions.q: The star sign and constellation Gemini is named after which twins?
questions.e: Its two brightest stars carry their names. In Greek myth, they shared immortality so they could stay together.

questions.q: James Joule, who gave us the unit of energy, was born on Christmas Eve 1818 and made his living from?
questions.e: Careful measuring in the family brewery helped him pin down heat and work. Science, with a side of beer.

questions.q: One food Calorie (kilocalorie) is about how many kilojoules?
questions.e: Different countries, different labels. Your mince pie doesn’t care which you use.

questions.q: Burning off one mince pie, at about 1000 kJ, takes roughly how long walking?
questions.e: Which is why Christmas Eve is the best time to take the dog for a very long walk.

questions.q: Scientists originally measured food’s energy by?
questions.a: Burning it in a sealed chamber
questions.e: A bomb calorimeter sets fire to your dinner under water, then checks how much hotter the water gets.

questions.q: Who popularised calorie counting with her 1918 bestseller, Diet and Health?
questions.e: It’s the first known diet bestseller. She’d lost a lot of weight herself and wrote it during World War I.

questions.q: Does turkey make you sleepy because of tryptophan?
questions.e: Turkey has about as much as chicken. It’s the huge meal, the wine and the family arguments.

questions.q: Since a 1970s ad campaign, a popular Christmas Eve dinner in Japan has been?
questions.e: People pre-order weeks ahead. Marketing is the most powerful holiday spirit of all.

questions.q: On Christmas Eve in Iceland, the tradition of ‘Jólabókaflóð’ means people give each other?
questions.e: It’s the ‘Christmas book flood’. People spend the night reading, ideally with chocolate.

questions.q: The Santa tracker now run by NORAD began in 1955, reportedly because?
questions.a: A newspaper ad misprinted a phone number
w: A pilot reported a strange sleigh
A radar test went badly wrong
questions.e: Children meant to ring a shop’s Santa rang a military hotline instead. The colonel played along.

questions.q: In the 1823 poem ‘A Visit from St. Nicholas’, two reindeer were named after Dutch words for thunder and lightning. They were first called?
questions.e: They later became Donder and Blitzen, and eventually Donner.

theme: Christmas with a nod to Newton

questions.q: Merry Christmas! Isaac Newton was born today in 1642, or on which date by our modern calendar?
questions.e: England was still on the old Julian calendar. Christmas Day baby by a technicality.

questions.q: Newton saw seven colours in the rainbow partly because he?
questions.a: Thought seven was a special number
w: Trained his eyes to see indigo
questions.e: Most people struggle to spot indigo. He added it and orange so the colours matched the seven notes of a musical scale.

questions.q: The Christmas cracker was invented in 1847 by?
questions.e: French bonbons wrapped in paper inspired him. The bang came later, and the terrible jokes after that.

questions.q: When tinsel was first made in Germany in the early 1600s, it was cut from?
questions.e: Silver looked gorgeous until it tarnished. Your plastic version is much cheaper, and much less shiny.

questions.q: The Gävle Goat, a giant straw goat in Sweden, is famous for?
questions.e: Since 1966, it has been set alight dozens of times despite the guards. Betting on its survival is a tradition.

questions.q: Catalonia’s Tió de Nadal is a Christmas log that children hit with sticks until it?
questions.e: They feed it for weeks, then sing to it and whack it. Yes, it has a smiling face.

questions.q: In 1965, the first song played in space was?
questions.e: Gemini 6 astronauts reported a sleigh in orbit, then played it on a smuggled harmonica and bells.

questions.q: Male reindeer usually drop their antlers in early winter. This means Santa’s antlered team were probably?
questions.e: Females keep theirs until spring. So give it up for Rudolph, who was probably a girl.

questions.q: ‘Mistletoe’ comes from Old English words often translated as?
questions.e: Birds spread the seeds in their droppings. Romantic, isn’t it?

questions.q: Iceland’s monstrous Yule Cat is said to eat people who don’t get what for Christmas?
questions.e: The old folk tale pushed families to finish the autumn wool work. New socks: more than just a boring gift.

questions.q: Marie and Pierre Curie announced radium on this day in 1898. The name comes from the Latin for?
questions.e: It glowed softly in the dark, which seemed delightful to people at the time.

questions.q: In 1940s Germany, Doramad toothpaste promised a brighter smile thanks to?
questions.e: It contained thorium-X, which is a radium isotope. It was said to help ‘gums and teeth’.

questions.q: The ‘Radium Girls’, who painted glow-in-the-dark watch dials, were taught to shape their brushes by?
questions.e: Many got very sick. Their brave court cases helped to establish workers’ safety rights.

questions.q: Radithor, sold in the USA in the 1920s, was?
questions.e: It was marketed as a health tonic until a famous customer’s death helped bring it down.

questions.q: The French radium cosmetics brand Tho-Radia claimed to use the formula of Dr Alfred Curie, who was?
questions.e: Just a helpful coincidence of surname, for marketing purposes.

questions.q: In 1950, a US toy company sold children a science kit that included?
questions.e: The Gilbert U-238 Atomic Energy Lab came with a Geiger counter. It didn’t sell well. Probably just as well.

questions.q: Roughly how long is the half-life of radium-226?
questions.e: Which is why Marie Curie’s notebooks will still be radioactive long after everyone reading this is gone.

questions.q: Which pretty old glass glows bright green under ultraviolet light?
questions.e: Collectors hunt for it with UV torches. It’s only faintly radioactive.

questions.q: In 1921, American women, led by journalist Missy Meloney, raised $100,000 to buy Marie Curie?
questions.e: President Harding handed it over in a special box. Her own lab had too little radium for its research.

questions.q: Today is also Boxing Day. It’s usually said to be named after?
questions.e: Servants and tradespeople got gifts the day after Christmas. Enjoy your leftovers.

theme: Germs and how we stop them

questions.q: The first known quarantine law, from 1377, was passed in Ragusa, now?
questions.e: It began with 30 days. Later, 40 days gave us the word, from the Italian ‘quaranta’.

questions.q: Mary Mallon, known as ‘Typhoid Mary’, was a cook in New York who?
w: Ran a famous New York restaurant
Caught typhoid more than ten times
questions.e: She felt well and didn’t believe she carried it. She spent decades in forced isolation, a sad story of its time.

questions.q: In 1721 Boston, an enslaved African man named Onesimus taught the town a way to prevent?
questions.e: He explained an African method of inoculation. Cotton Mather promoted it, and it saved many lives.

questions.q: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought smallpox inoculation to Britain after seeing it in?
questions.e: She had her own children inoculated and encouraged others, decades before Edward Jenner’s vaccine.

questions.q: The last natural case of smallpox was in 1977 in which country?
questions.e: In 1980 the WHO declared the world free of it, the first human disease to be eradicated.

questions.q: During the plague of 1665, villagers in Eyam, England, famously?
questions.e: People left coins in vinegar-filled holes in boundary stones in exchange for food. Many died to protect their neighbours.

questions.q: Does the nursery rhyme ‘Ring a Ring o’ Roses’ really describe the plague?
w: Yes, written by a London vicar
questions.e: The rhyme first appeared in print centuries later, and folklorists don’t buy the story.

questions.q: Why was the 1918 pandemic called the ‘Spanish flu’?
w: Its first victims were Spanish sailors
questions.e: Wartime countries hid their numbers, and neutral Spain did not. So Spain got the name, unfairly.

questions.q: Today, health workers can spot polio spreading through a city by testing?
questions.e: Germs tell tales. Wastewater shows what’s around before people get seriously ill.

questions.q: In 2014, Dr Stella Ameyo Adadevoh is credited with limiting Ebola in Nigeria by?
questions.a: Refusing to let an infected traveller leave
questions.e: She held firm under pressure, and it protected many people. She lost her own life to the disease.

questions.q: Stan Lee was born today in 1922 as?
questions.e: He split his first name to save his real one for the great novel he planned to write.

questions.q: Spider-Man got his powers from a bite by?
questions.e: Real-world advice: spider bites do not improve your wall-climbing.

questions.q: Weight for weight, real spider silk can be stronger than?
questions.e: It’s also far stretchier. Scientists are still trying to manufacture it properly.

questions.q: The real animal called a wolverine belongs to which family?
questions.e: It’s a very tough, big weasel. It can take on animals much larger than itself. The claws are real, too, though not metal.

questions.q: In his first comic in 1962, the Hulk was which colour?
questions.e: Printers couldn’t get the grey to look right, so he went green in the very next issue.

questions.q: Black Panther’s home country is called?
questions.e: Fictional, but the movie’s world is full of real African languages and designs.

questions.q: Wonder Woman’s creator, William Moulton Marston, also helped develop?
questions.e: It’s no accident she carries a Lasso of Truth. His wife Elizabeth also worked on the idea.

questions.q: In his early comics, Superman couldn’t fly. He could only?
questions.e: ‘Able to leap tall buildings in a single bound’ was accurate. The flying came later.

questions.q: Kamala Khan, a Pakistani American teenager from New Jersey, is known as?
questions.e: In 2014 she became the first Muslim character to headline her own Marvel comic.

questions.q: Marvel’s Daredevil has heightened senses, and he’s also?
questions.e: Matt Murdock’s other senses have been boosted by the same accident. He’s also a lawyer, the true superpower.

questions.q: Charles Goodyear’s big breakthrough in making rubber tough is said to have come when he dropped a mix on?
questions.e: He had spent years in debt chasing the idea. The process is called vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the god of fire.

questions.q: What’s the link between Charles Goodyear and the Goodyear Tire company?
questions.a: None, it was named after him later
w: He founded it on his birthday
His son became the first boss
He sold it for a fortune
questions.e: It was founded in 1898, nearly 40 years after he died, deeply in debt.

questions.q: Rubber got its English name because it could?
questions.e: Joseph Priestley pointed this out in 1770. Hardly a grand name for such a useful thing.

questions.q: Thousands of years before Goodyear, people in ancient Mexico were already using rubber to make?
questions.e: The Mesoamerican ballgame was huge. They had figured out a way to toughen rubber with plant juice.

questions.q: Gumboots are also known as Wellingtons after?
questions.e: The Duke of Wellington wore leather versions long before rubber took over. He’s also the one with the traffic cone.

questions.q: The first rubber balloons, in 1824, were made by scientist Michael Faraday for?
questions.e: He sealed two sheets of rubber together. Party shops can thank a physics lab.

questions.q: Car tyres are black because rubber has been mixed with?
questions.e: Natural rubber is pale. The carbon makes tyres last much longer.

questions.q: Bubble gum’s inventor, accountant Walter Diemer, made it pink because?
questions.a: Pink was the only dye he had
w: He wanted it to look healthy
questions.e: The first batch of bubble gum, in 1928, took the colour from whatever was on the shelf. It stuck, so to speak.

questions.q: Around 1890, some of the first thin rubber work gloves were ordered from Goodyear to protect?
questions.e: Harsh cleaning chemicals were hurting the nurse’s hands. Her boss, William Halsted, ordered the gloves, then married her. A very practical romance.

questions.q: Air-filled tyres were popularised in 1888 by Belfast vet John Dunlop, who made them for?
questions.e: He wanted a smoother ride for his son on bumpy roads. Then everyone else wanted one too.

questions.q: Tiger Woods, born today in 1975, has which real first name?
questions.e: ‘Tiger’ honours a Vietnamese soldier who was a friend of his father.

questions.q: At what age did Tiger Woods show off his putting on a US TV talk show?
questions.e: That’s younger than most people learn to use a fork.

questions.q: What do the dimples on a golf ball do?
questions.e: Dimples reduce drag. Golfers once noticed that old beat-up balls flew further than smooth new ones.

questions.q: Who hit a golf ball on the Moon in 1971?
questions.e: He sneaked a club head onto Apollo 14 and said it flew ‘miles and miles’. It went about 36 metres.

questions.q: Why did Scotland ban golf in 1457?
questions.a: It got in the way of archery practice
questions.e: Soldiers were supposed to be practising with their bows. Nobody listened.

questions.q: The story of Mary, Queen of Scots, golfing just days after her husband’s murder comes only from?
questions.e: She’s often called the mother of golf, but some historians think it was early fake news.

questions.q: In golf, what’s a ‘condor’?
questions.a: Four under par on a hole
questions.e: It’s rarer than an albatross, which is three under. It has happened only a handful of times.

questions.q: In 2001, who became the first woman to shoot a 59 in LPGA competition?
questions.e: The Swedish star earned the nickname ‘Ms 59’.

questions.q: At the World Ice Golf Championship in Greenland, the putting surfaces are known as?
questions.e: There are no greens. Balls are pink, orange or red, for obvious reasons.

questions.q: The golf tee was patented in 1899 by Boston dentist George Franklin Grant, who was also?
questions.a: The first Black professor at Harvard
w: The first man to climb Mont Blanc
questions.e: Before tees, golfers built a small heap of sand each time. He also made a major contribution to treating cleft palate.

questions.q: In Spain, people mark midnight on New Year’s Eve by eating?
questions.e: One for each chime of the clock. It’s harder than it sounds, especially when you’re laughing.

questions.q: In Denmark, a traditional way to show friends you care on New Year’s Eve is to?
questions.e: The bigger the pile outside, the more friends you have. Please sweep.

questions.q: Which colour is the hardest to get right in fireworks?
questions.e: Copper compounds are fussy about temperature. Pretty, and very hard.

questions.q: Why did New York start dropping a ball in Times Square in 1907?
w: A ship had signalled the time this way
A shop wanted to sell lamps
It was a mistake by a workman
questions.e: Ball drops were an old way of signalling time to ships, and the organisers needed a replacement show.

questions.q: Samoa hopped across the International Date Line in 2011 and skipped which date?
questions.e: It moved closer to trading partners Australia and New Zealand. Somebody’s birthday just vanished.

questions.q: Dark drinks like whiskey and red wine can leave a worse hangover because of chemicals called?
questions.e: They’re by-products of fermenting, and darker drinks tend to have more. Colour is only a clue, though.

questions.q: Barbe-Nicole Clicquot, the ‘widow’ of Veuve Clicquot, invented what to make champagne clear?
questions.e: A widow at 27, she took over the business and changed champagne forever. Dom Pérignon, by the way, didn’t invent it.

questions.q: A sealed bottle of champagne holds pressure about how many times a car tyre’s?
questions.e: So, yes, point it away from Grandma.

questions.q: In Scottish Hogmanay tradition, the ‘first-foot’ over your doorstep after midnight should ideally?
questions.a: Bring a gift, such as coal
questions.e: A tall, dark stranger bearing coal, whisky or shortbread brings good luck, or so they say.

questions.q: In Colombia and elsewhere in Latin America, people hoping to travel next year will walk around the block carrying?
questions.e: Happy New Year. Best to check your passport too.
